Respectful Plural Address ('-i') & Calling Etiquette in Shona

When calling someone over in Zimbabwe ('Huyai kuno!'), both grammar and body language express respect. Adding '-i' to 'huya' ('huyai') honors an elder, parent, or group. Culturally, when gesturing for someone to come closer with your hand, you always beckon with your palm facing downward—beckoning with the palm facing upward or curling a single index finger is considered impolite.

Children's Role & Helping Parents ('Kubatsira Vabereki') at Home

In Shona family life, children grow up participating in daily household tasks alongside their mother ('amai') and father ('baba')—from fetching utensils and sweeping the yard ('kutsvaira chivanze') to helping prepare meals. Learning to respond warmly when a parent says 'Chiuya kuno undibatsire' ('Come here now and help me') is considered a cornerstone of 'hunhu' (good character and upbringing).

Celebrating Shared Milestones ('Makorokoto!') in the Community

Whenever someone graduates, starts a new job, welcomes a baby, or achieves a life goal, relatives and neighbours gather to say 'Makorokoto nekubudirira kwenyu!' ('Congratulations on your success!'). In Zimbabwean culture, an individual's success belongs to the whole extended family, and celebrations are often accompanied by joyful ululation ('kupururudza' by women) and rhythmic clapping ('kuuchira' by men).

Home Security, Evening Breezes & the Highveld Climate

Much of Zimbabwe sits on a high central plateau ('Highveld') between 1,200 and 1,500 metres above sea level. Because of this elevation, brisk winds and cool evening air are common even after warm afternoons, and households habitually remind one another to close the door firmly ('vhara musuwo zvakasimba') when stepping outside.

The Evening Family Meal ('Chirairo') & Shared Dining Etiquette

In Zimbabwean homes, the evening meal ('chirairo' or 'kudya kwemanheru') is the main social gathering of the day. Family members make a special effort to return home before dinner ('tisati tadya manheru') so everyone can sit together, wash hands from a shared water jug and basin ('chirongo nedhishi'), and exchange news of the day.

The word 'musha' (locative 'kumusha') means both 'home' and the ancestral rural homestead. Most Zimbabweans who work in towns or cities maintain deep roots in their rural 'kumusha', returning regularly on weekends and holidays after finishing work ('kana wapedza basa') to tend family land and visit elders.

A hearty morning meal is essential before starting school or farm work. Alongside tea and bread, the classic Zimbabwean breakfast is 'bota'—a smooth, thinner maize or finger-millet porridge ('bota rezviyo') stirred with a dollop of rich homemade roasted peanut butter ('dovi'), or boiled sweet potatoes ('mbambaira') and pumpkin ('manhanga').

This single sentence names the four most essential grocery items in any Zimbabwean household: white maize meal ('hupfu') for cooking 'sadza', sugar ('shuga') for morning and afternoon tea, cooking oil ('mafuta') for sautéing relishes, and fresh leafy greens ('muriwo'—such as 'chomolia', rape, or mustard greens 'tsunga') harvested daily from the garden or market.

Slow-Braised Traditional Meats & 'Gocho' (Braai) Culture

In Zimbabwean cooking, free-range rural chicken ('huku yechivanhu' or 'roadrunner') and pasture-raised beef ('nyama yemombe') or goat ('nyama yembudzi') have a firmer texture and deeper flavour than commercial meats. Cooks simmer the meat slowly with water and salt until tender before letting it brown in its own natural fat ('kukanga').

Buying a family car ('mota' or 'motokari') is a major milestone in Zimbabwe. Most personal vehicles on Zimbabwean roads are fuel-efficient Japanese sedans and small trucks imported via ports in Dar es Salaam (Tanzania), Durban (South Africa), or Beira (Mozambique) and driven across the border posts at Chirundu, Beitbridge, or Forbes.

Freshly baked loaves of bread ('chingwa') from local bakeries like Lobels or Proton are a daily staple in Zimbabwean homes. Commuters returning from work ('pandinobva kubasa') routinely stop by their neighbourhood 'chitoro' (shop) in the late afternoon to pick up a fresh loaf for the next morning's breakfast.

drills.prompt: Translate this new greeting into English: 'Masikati amai, maswera zvakanaka here?'

drills.prompt: Complete this new sentence in the past tense: 'Nezuro amai ______ sadza nenyama.' (Yesterday Mother cooked sadza and meat.)

drills.prompt: If someone says 'Ndinonzwa nyota, ndinoda kunwa mukaka kana mvura', what are they asking for?

distractors: Bread and sugar because it is morning
Maize meal and cooking oil from the market
Salt and vegetables for the evening meal

drills.prompt: Choose the natural English meaning of this new sentence: 'Vana vanoda kudya chingwa nemukaka mangwanani.'

distractors: We bought sugar, salt, and vegetables yesterday.
Father is cooking meat and sadza for dinner tonight.
The bread has run out so I am going to the shop.

drills.prompt: How do you say 'Add a little salt to the vegetables' in Shona?
drills.correct: Isa munyu mushoma mumuriwo.
drills.explanation: 'Isa' = 'Put/add', 'munyu mushoma' = 'a little salt', 'mumuriwo' = 'in the vegetables'.

drills.prompt: In 'Hupfu hwapera mumba', why does 'hwapera' ('has run out') start with 'hwa-'?
drills.correct: Because 'hupfu' (maize meal) belongs to the 'hu-' noun group, which uses 'hwa-' in the recent past
distractors: Because it refers to a person cooking in the kitchen
drills.explanation: Nouns starting with 'hu-' (like 'hupfu') use 'hu-' / 'hwa-' subject prefixes on the verb.

drills.prompt: Translate this new kitchen sentence into English: 'Tichatenga mafuta ekubikisa nemadomasi pamusika.'
drills.correct: We will buy cooking oil and tomatoes at the market.
distractors: They cooked sadza and green vegetables for the guests.
Please pour warm milk into the child's cup.
I ate roasted groundnuts and sweet potatoes at home.
drills.explanation: 'Tichatenga' = 'We will buy', 'mafuta ekubikisa' = 'cooking oil', 'nemadomasi' = 'and tomatoes', 'pamusika' = 'at the market'.

drills.prompt: How do you describe 'a white shirt and black shoes' in Shona?
drills.correct: hembe chena neshangu nhema
drills.explanation: 'Hembe chena' = 'white shirt', 'ne-' = 'and', and 'shangu nhema' = 'black shoes'.

drills.prompt: Complete this sentence about tree leaves: 'Mashizha emuti uyu ane ruvara ______.' (The leaves of this tree have a green colour.)
drills.correct: rwegirinhi
drills.explanation: 'Ruvara rwegirinhi' expresses 'green colour' when describing fresh leaves ('mashizha').

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Mukoma wangu akatenga mota chena nezuro.'
drills.correct: My older brother bought a white car yesterday.
distractors: My sister is wearing a red dress today.
Which bus goes to the city centre?
The black truck is parked beside the road.
drills.explanation: 'Mukoma wangu' = 'My older brother', 'akatenga' = 'bought', 'mota chena' = 'a white car', 'nezuro' = 'yesterday'.

drills.prompt: Why is 'white' written as 'chena' in 'hembe chena' (white shirt), but 'machena' in 'mabhuku machena' (white books)?
drills.correct: Colour adjectives change their prefix to match the noun they describe ('ma-' for 'mabhuku')
distractors: 'Machena' means light grey while 'chena' means bright white
Only clothing can use the word 'chena'
'Machena' is only used in the past tense
drills.explanation: In Shona, traditional colour stems (-chena, -tema, -tsvuku) take the prefix of the noun they describe.

drills.prompt: Which sentence means 'The girl is wearing a yellow hat and a blue dress'?
drills.correct: Musikana akapfeka ngowani yeyero nerokwe rebhuruu.
distractors: Mukomana akapfeka bhachi dema neshangu tsvuku.
Mbatya dzose dziri kuoma pamutambo panze.
drills.explanation: 'Ngowani yeyero' = 'a yellow hat', and 'nerokwe rebhuruu' = 'and a blue dress'.

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Ndeipi shangu yaunoda, nhema kana tsvuku?'
drills.correct: Which shoe do you want, the black one or the red one?
distractors: Where did you put my white shirt and blue trousers?
These new shoes are very comfortable for walking.
She washed all the white clothes this morning.
drills.explanation: 'Ndeipi shangu yaunoda' = 'Which shoe do you want', 'nhema kana tsvuku' = 'the black one or the red one'.

drills.prompt: Which phrase correctly translates 'three books' in Shona? (Hint: 'mabhuku' is a 'ma-' plural noun.)
drills.correct: mabhuku matatu
drills.explanation: The number stem '-tatu' (three) takes the 'ma-' prefix to match 'mabhuku' -> 'mabhuku matatu'.

drills.prompt: How do you say 'two women and four men' in Shona?
drills.correct: vakadzi vaviri nevarume vana
drills.explanation: 'Vakadzi vaviri' = 'two women' (-viri = 2) and 'nevarume vana' = 'and four men' (-na = 4).

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Tine mabhuku mana patafura.'
drills.correct: We have four books on the table.
distractors: There are three cups in the kitchen.
Wait here for five minutes please.
drills.explanation: 'Tine' = 'We have', 'mabhuku mana' = 'four books', 'patafura' = 'on the table'.

drills.prompt: How do you form ordinal numbers like 'first', 'second', and 'third' in Shona?
drills.correct: Attach '-ekutanga' (first), '-echipiri' (second), and '-echitatu' (third) with the noun's possessive prefix
distractors: Place the word 'nhamba' after the verb
drills.explanation: Ordinal numbers use '-ekutanga' (1st), '-echipiri' (2nd), '-echitatu' (3rd), e.g., 'zuva rechitatu' ('the third day').

drills.prompt: Why do we say 'miti mitatu' for 'three trees' but 'zvigaro zvitatu' for 'three chairs'?
drills.correct: The number stem '-tatu' takes 'mi-' for 'miti' (trees) and 'zvi-' for 'zvigaro' (chairs)
distractors: Because trees are taller than chairs
Because 'mitatu' means thirty and 'zvitatu' means three
Because 'miti' is singular and 'zvigaro' is plural
drills.explanation: Numbers 1–5 mirror the prefix of the noun they count: 'miti mitatu', 'zvigaro zvitatu', 'vanhu vatatu'.

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Chitima chichasvika mushure memaminitsi mashanu.'
drills.correct: The train will arrive after five minutes.
distractors: We waited at the bus stop for two hours.
Three buses left the station this morning.
This is my third time visiting Masvingo.
drills.explanation: 'Chitima chichasvika' = 'The train will arrive', 'mushure memaminitsi mashanu' = 'after five minutes'.

drills.prompt: Choose the right locative prefix: You want to say 'The keys are ON the table' ('______tafura').
drills.correct: patafura
drills.explanation: The prefix 'pa-' means 'on / at a specific surface', so 'pa-' + 'tafura' = 'patafura' ('on the table').

drills.prompt: What is the difference between 'mumba' and 'panze'?
drills.correct: 'mumba' means inside the house, while 'panze' means outside
distractors: 'mumba' means at school, while 'panze' means at work
'mumba' means on the roof, while 'panze' means in the kitchen
'mumba' means rural village, while 'panze' means city centre
drills.explanation: 'Mu-' denotes 'inside' ('mumba' = inside the house), whereas 'panze' means 'outside in the yard'.

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Baba vari mumba asi vana vari kutamba panze.'
drills.correct: Father is in the house, but the children are playing outside.
distractors: Mother went to the market to buy fruit and vegetables.
The books and keys are lying on the table.
We are going to the rural home tomorrow morning.
drills.explanation: 'Baba vari mumba' = 'Father is in the house', 'asi' = 'but', 'vana vari kutamba panze' = 'the children are playing outside'.

drills.prompt: Which locative word means 'in the kitchen'?
drills.correct: mukicheni
drills.explanation: Adding 'mu-' ('inside') to 'kicheni' ('kitchen') gives 'mukicheni' ('in/inside the kitchen').

drills.prompt: How do you say 'There is a cup of water on the table' in Shona?
drills.correct: Patafura pane kapu yemvura.
drills.explanation: 'Patafura' ('on the table') pairs with 'pane' ('there is at/on that spot') + 'kapu yemvura' ('a cup of water').

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Ndasiya nharembozha yangu pachigaro mumba yokutandarira.'
drills.correct: I left my mobile phone on the chair in the living room.
distractors: Please close the door and all the windows before sleeping.
My keys are inside the small bag on the table.
We are sitting under the shade tree outside the house.
drills.explanation: 'Ndasiya' = 'I left', 'nharembozha yangu' = 'my mobile phone', 'pachigaro' = 'on the chair', 'mumba yokutandarira' = 'in the living room'.

drills.prompt: Complete this sentence using the Present Progressive ('is reading right now'): 'Shamwari yangu ______ bhuku idzva.'
drills.correct: iri kuverenga
drills.explanation: 'Shamwari' uses the progressive form 'iri ku-' + '-verenga' (read) to mean 'is reading right now'.

drills.prompt: Why do we say 'Mbuya vari kurima' instead of 'Mbuya ari kurima' when talking about one grandmother?
drills.correct: Shona uses the plural prefix 'va-' ('vari') to show polite respect to elders and parents
distractors: Because 'mbuya' always refers to three or more people
Because 'vari' is only used for the future tense
Because 'ari' can only be used with inanimate objects
drills.explanation: In Shona, respected family elders ('amai', 'baba', 'mbuya', 'sekuru') always take the polite plural 'va-' agreement.

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Vana vari kudzidzira kunyora bvunzo kuchikoro.'
drills.correct: The children are practicing to write examinations at school.
distractors: The teacher gave us new books yesterday morning.
My grandmother grows groundnuts and maize at the rural home.
My friend called me after finishing work today.
drills.explanation: 'Vana vari kudzidzira' = 'The children are practicing', 'kunyora bvunzo' = 'to write exams', 'kuchikoro' = 'at school'.

drills.prompt: How do you say 'Our teacher teaches us Shona every day'?
drills.correct: Mudzidzisi wedu anotirayiridza ChiShona mazuva ose.
drills.explanation: 'Mudzidzisi wedu' = 'Our teacher', 'anotirayiridza' = 'teaches/instructs us', 'mazuva ose' = 'every day'.

drills.prompt: Which possessive word means 'our grandmother'?
drills.correct: mbuya vedu
drills.explanation: Because 'mbuya' takes the respectful 'va-' agreement, 'our grandmother' is 'mbuya vedu' ('va-' + '-edu').

drills.prompt: Translate this new family sentence into English: 'Hanzvadzi yangu inoshanda muguta reHarare.'
drills.correct: My sibling works in the city of Harare.
distractors: My parents live at the rural homestead in Masvingo.
My friend passed all her school examinations this year.
The baby is sleeping quietly inside the bedroom.
drills.explanation: 'Hanzvadzi yangu' = 'My sibling (brother/sister)', 'inoshanda' = 'works', 'muguta reHarare' = 'in the city of Harare'.

drills.prompt: Complete this future weather forecast: 'Mangwana zuva ______ zvakanaka.' (Tomorrow the sun will shine brightly.)
drills.correct: richabuda
drills.explanation: 'Zuva' (sun) takes the prefix 'ri-' + future marker '-cha-' + '-buda' (come out/shine) -> 'richabuda'.

drills.prompt: If a farmer says 'Gore rino takawana goho guru pamunda pedu', what happened?
drills.correct: They obtained a big harvest from their field this year
distractors: They are waiting for the rain to start next month
The river flooded and washed away the bridge
A strong wind blew from the east all afternoon
drills.explanation: 'Takawana' = 'we obtained/got', 'goho guru' = 'a big harvest', 'pamunda pedu' = 'from our field'.

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Mhepo iri kuvhuvhuta uye mvura ichanaya manheru.'
drills.correct: The wind is blowing and it will rain in the evening.
distractors: The river is full of water after yesterday's heavy rain.
Tall green trees grow along the sides of the mountain.
The dog barked outside when it saw the visitors.
drills.explanation: 'Mhepo iri kuvhuvhuta' = 'The wind is blowing', 'uye' = 'and', 'mvura ichanaya manheru' = 'it will rain in the evening'.

drills.prompt: How do you say 'Tall trees and green grass' in Shona?
drills.correct: miti mirefu neuswa hwegirinhi
drills.explanation: 'Miti mirefu' = 'tall trees' (plural 'mi-' agreement on '-refu'), and 'neuswa hwegirinhi' = 'and green grass'.

drills.prompt: In 'Shiri diki dziri kuimba pamusoro pemuti', what are the small birds doing?
drills.correct: Singing at the top of the tree
distractors: Looking for seeds in the field
drills.explanation: 'Shiri diki' = 'small birds', 'dziri kuimba' = 'are singing', 'pamusoro pemuti' = 'at the top of the tree'.

drills.prompt: Translate this new nature sentence into English: 'Makomo makuru anoonekwa kure seri kwerwizi.'
drills.correct: Large mountains can be seen far away beyond the river.
distractors: Two rhinoceroses are grazing peacefully in the valley.
The farmers planted maize and groundnuts after the rain.
Dark clouds have covered the sky this afternoon.
drills.explanation: 'Makomo makuru' = 'Large mountains', 'anoonekwa' = 'are seen / can be seen', 'kure seri kwerwizi' = 'far away beyond the river'.

drills.prompt: In a Zimbabwean city, if a driver says 'Mota dzakamira parobhoti dzichimirira mwenje wegirinhi', where are the cars stopped?
drills.correct: At the traffic light waiting for the green light
distractors: At a rural bus stop waiting for passengers
Inside a garage having their tyres repaired
Beside a river bridge that is under construction
drills.explanation: 'Robhoti' (plural 'marobhotsi') is the standard Shona word for a traffic light, and 'mwenje wegirinhi' is the green light.

drills.prompt: Complete this sentence about travelling: 'Mangwana ______ bhazi rinoenda kuMasvingo.' (Tomorrow we will board the bus going to Masvingo.)
drills.correct: tichakwira
drills.explanation: 'Ti-' (we) + '-cha-' (future 'will') + '-kwira' (board/climb) = 'tichakwira' ('we will board').

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Kombi chena iri kufamba pamugwagwa mukuru.'
drills.correct: The white minibus is travelling along the main road.
distractors: The large red truck is parked at the fuel station.
Two people are standing beside the shop in town.
Our journey to the mountains was long but enjoyable.
drills.explanation: 'Kombi chena' = 'The white minibus', 'iri kufamba' = 'is travelling', 'pamugwagwa mukuru' = 'along the main road'.

drills.prompt: What does 'parutivi pemugwagwa' mean in 'Rori yakamira parutivi pemugwagwa'?
drills.correct: Beside the road / on the side of the road
distractors: In the middle of the intersection
drills.explanation: 'Parutivi pe-' means 'beside / at the side of', and 'mugwagwa' is 'road'.

drills.prompt: How do you say 'Our journey was very good' in Shona?
drills.correct: Rwendo rwedu rwakanga rwakanaka kwazvo.
drills.explanation: 'Rwendo rwedu' = 'Our journey' (taking 'rw-' agreement), 'rwakanga rwakanaka kwazvo' = 'was very good'.

drills.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Vanhu vakamira pamusika vachimirira kukwira bhazi.'
drills.correct: People are standing at the market waiting to board the bus.
distractors: The driver stopped the car near the traffic lights.
We saw two large trucks carrying maize to the city.
The road to the eastern highlands has many curves.
drills.explanation: 'Vanhu vakamira pamusika' = 'People are standing at the market', 'vachimirira kukwira bhazi' = 'waiting to board the bus'.
